Also, I've been playing with speech models for the past 2 years, and for me anything below 8-bit is a huge drop in quality; so quantisation for LLMs and for other bespoke modality models, is not 1:1.

comments.author: billypilgrim
comments.text:
When I had started my PhD, I thought the writing part of a paper was just the last thing I needed to do to summarize my results, like a boring epilogue to the more exciting science. What surprised me was how much of the scientific process relied on my ability to convey my ideas to someone else. And to be able to do that you need clarity of mind, you need to have worked through multiple drafts to be able to get to your point as efficiently and clearly as possible. So many times I only discovered what I was
actually
researching during the writing part.
The problem with AI writing is that it makes people believe that writing is just writing and not a tool for thinking very deeply about the topic you are writing about. I am not completely opposed to AI assisted writing, but if I see AI writing, it’s telling me that the author tried to take a shortcut in their own thinking and it’s a good heuristic that the ideas will not be thought through enough to warrant my complete attention.

comments.author: theptip
comments.text:
Writing is a good thinking tool.
But, to the claim of how to think in the age of LLMs, I think it’s worth contrasting the other approach, which is a dialog with the LLM; two things are needed IMO to keep things honest:
First, you need to keep asking the LLM to explain things, until you understand what it did. Lots of angles here; have the LLM make a design/product doc, write one-off architecture explainers, write throwaway data-viz tools to explain the data distribution. Then ask a fresh copy to adversarially review the core concepts. Try asking a different frontier model too.
Second, you need to push for “proof”, in other words, ask for demos and try it yourself. Imagine yourself a CEO or VC; how do you know if the output of an entire org is vaporware? One thing to beware is launching into a field where you don’t have expertise and can’t actually validate the output. This takes time of course, but for example if you write a stress test script and get CPU/QPS numbers, these complex validators are IME quite reliable when you apply the same rigor from 1) above to their construction.

comments.author: bottlepalm
comments.text:
I used to use ChatGPT/Claude in the TUI up until like 3 months ago, but my usage of LLMs has exploded - many sessions across many projects. I feel like I outgrew the TUI and now I'm using ChatGPT/Claude desktop. VS Code has become a code review tool and place where I manage git if need be.
The GUI is less verbose with the nitty gritty hidden in expandable sections, which makes history easier and cleaner to scroll through, also no scrolling bugs, rich text is easier to read with tables, and images integrated into the chat, resources like browsers in the context of the session. Drag and drop session organization (pins), scheduled tasks, etc.. all that in the side bar.
Usually a TUI would be open in VS Code and scoped to whatever repo I'm working with so 10 projects, 10 VS Code instances open, not super scalable. With the GUI desktop app it's one app, and I can start sessions in an repo and switch between them easily, no need to open VS Code for each. I don't see what could make me want to go back to using a TUI.
Who else is just using the GUI nowadays, or are you still on the TUI, and why, have you tried the GUI interfaces?

comments.author: drfuchs
comments.text: For prior related work, check out patent US-6377261-B1 "Compiling glyphs into instructions for imaging for execution on a general purpose computer" filed 1996.  The basic idea is each character turns into a sequence of "Load Immediate" / "Shift" / "OR to Memory" instructions; so there's no more fetching from a stored bitmap of the font, as the pixels are implicit in the Immediate data in the generated machine code.  Then you can get fancy when one row of pixels is the same as the previous row in the character, so you don't even need to do the Load Immediate.  Etc.  This scheme was used in FrameMaker for Macintosh back in the day, as implemented by Gus Fernandez (who went hog wild on additional optimizations).

comments.author: karmakaze
comments.text:
This is a really great project. So many retro computers are OP that they can use large frame buffers and programming to them doesn't feel like being close to the metal back like back in the day which was more intimate.
This implementation reminds me of two of my early experiences: programming display lists on Atari 8-bit and an HP PCL 5e interpreter
(with short raster band buffer)
. I didn't really get into VCS/2600 128-byte beam racing but did do a fair amount of display-list-interrupt on-the-fly coding for homemade games and demos. I really thought the Atari Antic display list system was terrific--thanks to Jay Miner who also did the Amiga--and didn't see much like it again until OS/2 Presentation Manager or Java FX.
The PCL interpreter probably had the closest shape using a few hundred line cyclic buffer. It 'rendered' into y-sorted objects that needed to be later rendered/rasterized. Each object was cut to be at most 255 pixels (0.85") tall and used reverse max-y ordering since it couldn't be drawn until after the beam passed the wraparound scan line still rendering Y - buffer_height.

comments.author: codazoda

I've been building BASIC32, a retro BASIC interpreter for microcontrollers so I can flash it once and easily create lots of new projects.
What you give up with the authors approach is "read". The screen becomes write-only. There are only a few functions that require reads: getting a pixels current color and doing operations like flood fills or paints.
Because I was going for the retro feel of BASIC, I wanted to support these, so I opted for a frame buffer. It isn't as technically cool. On the RP2350, it does require low resolution and low bit rates because they often have RAM limited to KB.
If you step-up to the ESP32-S3 variants with 4MB or 8MB of RAM the frame buffer gets much easier.

comments.author: bcherny
comments.text:
Boris from the Claude Code team here. Historically Claude Code has not done secret scrubbing (there are many good tools for that), but we are looking into what we can do to prevent this.
That said, a few thoughts:
1. .claude/settings.local.json is meant to stay local. This is not a file you should check into source control. We automatically gitignore it when Claude creates the file, so in this case the files were manually created and checked in (docs:
https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings
)
2. Permission rules are old hat. Everyone should be using auto mode instead. It is safer and also does not require manually maintaining finicky allow/deny lists. Auto mode is enabled by default and is included for free in all plans.
3. Regardless of what agent you use, you should have secret scanning enabled. GitHub and other source control hosts offer it. There are many threat models that it protects against and you should absolutely use it if you can. (see
https://github.com/security/plans
)

comments.author: tsergiu
comments.text:
I'm super paranoid about the level of access AI agents have. At the same time, I want them to take away the tedium of a bunch of tasks I'm required to do, and it sucks to have to micromanage them.
The best solution I've been able to come up is using an ephemeral vm (on an isolated network) per task, using --dangerously-skip-permissions so it doesn't bother me. I couple that with an API proxy that lets me restrict the permissions it has to external services. So e.g. where a quickbooks API key gives the holder "god mode" access, the proxy lets the agent do certain read commands without confirmation, but all write endpoints except uploading receipts require confirmation on my phone before they'll be allowed to hit the quickbooks servers. I no longer need to trust that the agent will interpret my readonly wishes correctly.
Tooting my own horn here, but this setup works incredibly well! I've been able to connect dozens of services safely where I absolutely do not trust giving raw, overpowered credentials or oauth integration to the agent directly. I actually just released the API proxy today at
https://keycontain.com

comments.author: anatolii1309

Two rules that stuck for us: secrets go into commands only via env vars ($TOKEN, never the value), and .claude/ lives in the machine-wide global gitignore, not in the repo. With those, "Don't ask again" is fine and a commit has nothing to leak.

comments.author: kqr
comments.text:
This is a great example of how to test how well a benchmark score generalises. The first order approximation is not complicated: just vary a parameter and see how much the score changes.
Which parameter to vary depends on the result of the test, but the MaxxBench route of varying the task spec seems like a good default, though not always the most informative.
In one of my private benchmarks I realised many of the less capable models didn't fail because they submitted the wrong answer, but because they exceeded their budget for number of tool calls they were allowed. The more capable models never got close to the tool call limit because they tended toward combining tool calls (e.g. chaining multiple shell commands in one Bash tool call).
Was my benchmark actually measuring ability to combine tool calls rather than reasoning ability on the problem at hand? Well, easy enough to find out: re-run under a different tool call budget and see how much the scores change.
(Next problem: is ability to combine tool calls a useful thing to measure, i.e.
should
it confer an advantage in the benchmark? It could be if it is a sign of planning multiple steps ahead.)

stories.title_en: Mizu – zero-copy parallel R and Python over shared memory

comments.author: stdbrouw
comments.text: Amazing. I remember being really disappointed in mirai last year when learning that it couldn’t provide shared access to an in-memory arrow table. Multicore processing in R is great when it works but too often it’s just a matter of time before unwanted and unnecessary data copies completely destroy performance.

comments.author: shikokuchuo
comments.text:
Author here: I wrote mizu (R) and pymizu (Python), packages that offer lock-free async and parallel computing over shared memory, built on the same C core, libmizu. The link above is for the Python package.
A task round trip drops to under one microsecond, from around 100 µs over sockets with Python's ProcessPoolExecutor or mirai, my other R framework. These are numbers from my laptop (an M4 Pro), and benchmark scripts are in the repos for you to run.
Workers claim tasks off lock-free queues, there is no task dispatcher, and system calls are avoided on the hot path.
`PoolExecutor` is a drop-in `concurrent.futures.Executor`, tasks are awaitable in asyncio, NumPy arrays and polars, pyarrow and pandas frames cross as zero-copy views. As mizu and pymizu share the same wire format, data frames and Arrow types also cross zero-copy between worker pools of different languages.
Of course, this is single-machine only as it uses shared memory. The API is still experimental. Usability feedback and bug reports are most welcome at the repos. I'd love to hear about places you'd like to see this used.
Write-up with full benchmarks and the R/Python code examples:
https://opensource.posit.co/blog/20
